Name: Longjing
Story (Legend or background): Imperial tribute tea from Hangzhou, legend says the Qianlong Emperor named eighteen bushes at Lion Peak after visiting disguised as a commoner.

Name: Bi Luo Chun
Story (Legend or background): Named for its curled snail-like leaves, traditionally planted among fruit trees in Dongting Lake region so blossoms scent the tea.

Name: Huangshan Maofeng
Story (Legend or background): Picked on misty Huangshan peaks in Anhui, 'mao feng' means furry peak, describing tender downy buds.

Name: Lu'an Guapian
Story (Legend or background): Unique melon-seed shaped leaves without buds or stems, listed among China's top ten famous teas since the Qing dynasty.

Name: Xinyang Maojian
Story (Legend or background): One of China's oldest named green teas from Henan, praised in Tang poetry for its sharp aroma and clean finish.

Name: Enshi Yulu
Story (Legend or background): Rare Chinese steamed green tea from Hubei, influenced by Japanese sencha methods while keeping native cultivars.

Name: Mengding Ganlu
Story (Legend or background): From sacred Mengding Mountain in Sichuan where Buddhist monk Wu Lizhen is said to have planted tea for the Han dynasty court.

Name: Taiping Houkui
Story (Legend or background): Extra-long flat leaves from two leaves and one bud, won gold at the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition and remains a gift tea icon.

Name: Anji Baicha
Story (Legend or background): High-amino acid cultivar discovered in the 1980s in Zhejiang, pale leaves and fresh umami made it a modern celebrity green.

Name: Gunpowder
Story (Legend or background): Rolled pellet tea from Zhejiang exported worldwide since the Ming era, name comes from its resemblance to black powder grains.

Name: Chunmee
Story (Legend or background): Curved eyebrow-shaped leaves from Anhui and Jiangxi, backbone of everyday Chinese green tea exports for centuries.

Name: Bai Hao Yin Zhen
Story (Legend or background): Only bud tea from Fuding and Zhenghe, Empress Dowager Cixi favored delicate white teas from Fujian workshops.

Name: Bai Mu Dan
Story (Legend or background): One bud with two leaves, peony-like open leaves when wet. Represents the middle grade of Fujian white tea tradition.

Name: Shou Mei
Story (Legend or background): Mature leaves and stems give a fuller, honeyed cup, originally the everyday white tea of local farmers.

Name: Gong Mei
Story (Legend or background): Historically a tribute grade between Peony and Shou Mei, today often grouped with Shou Mei in export markets.

Name: Ya Bao
Story (Legend or background): Not true tea but wild Camellia buds from Yunnan forests, sweet resinous notes prized by pu-erh enthusiasts.

Name: Junshan Yinzhen
Story (Legend or background): From Dongting Lake island, rare yellow tea with bud-only picking. Said to have been reserved for Mao Zedong as a state gift.

Name: Mengding Huangya
Story (Legend or background): Sichuan yellow tea with sealed-yellowing process, linked to the same Mengding Mountain origin myths as Mengding Ganlu.

Name: Huoshan Huangya
Story (Legend or background): Anhui yellow tea revived in the 20th century, Tang records mention yellow teas from Huoshan as imperial offerings.

Name: Tie Guan Yin
Story (Legend or background): Anxi oolong named after Guanyin, legend tells of a poor farmer who restored a temple and received this tea plant in a dream.

Name: Da Hong Pao
Story (Legend or background): Legend says red robes were draped on Wuyi bushes to cure an imperial student's illness, mother trees still famous on Jiulongke cliff.

Name: Wuyi Rougui
Story (Legend or background): Rock tea cultivar with spicy cinnamon aroma from mineral-rich Wuyi cliffs, one of the Four Famous Bushes of Wuyi.

Name: Wuyi Shui Xian
Story (Legend or background): Old bush Shui Xian from Wuyi carries deep floral-narcissus notes, name may refer to Narcissus oolong or a local spring spirit tale.

Name: Wuyi Qi Lan
Story (Legend or background): Cultivar prized for orchid fragrance among rock teas, developed through selective breeding of Wuyi native varieties.

Name: Wuyi Ba Xian
Story (Legend or background): Named after the Eight Taoist Immortals, each cultivar line in Wuyi carries a story tying tea to local folklore.

Name: Fenghuang Dan Cong – Mi Lan Xiang
Story (Legend or background): Phoenix Mountain oolong with honey-orchid aroma, Dan Cong means single bush, each tree cloned for a unique scent profile.

Name: Fenghuang Dan Cong – Ya Shi Xiang
Story (Legend or background): Intentionally vulgar name to hide prized bushes from theft, actually a bright floral oolong with no duck involved.

Name: Dong Ding Oolong
Story (Legend or background): Taiwanese high-mountain style rooted in Fujian, named after Dong Ding mountain where tea was brought by immigrants in the 19th century.

Name: Oriental Beauty
Story (Legend or background): Taiwanese oolong where leafhopper bites create honey notes, presented as 'Oriental Beauty' to Queen Elizabeth II in the 1960s.

Name: Ali Shan High Mountain Oolong
Story (Legend or background): Grown above 1000 m in Taiwan's Alishan range, cool mist slows growth and concentrates sweetness in tight rolled leaves.

Name: Golden Osmanthus Oolong
Story (Legend or background): Anxi-style oolong scented with osmanthus flowers, popular autumn tea in Fujian and Guangdong banquets.

Name: Zheng Shan Xiao Zhong
Story (Legend or background): From Tongmu village where pine-smoking was said to dry tea quickly when armies passed through during the late Ming turmoil.

Name: Qimen Hong Cha
Story (Legend or background): Anhui black tea created in 1875 that became the base of English Breakfast blends, winey aroma won prizes at 1915 Panama Expo.

Name: Dian Hong – Golden Needle
Story (Legend or background): Yunnan large-leaf cultivar buds turned into golden tippy red tea, developed in the 20th century for export and gift markets.

Name: Jinjunmei
Story (Legend or background): Luxury lapsang-region black tea of tiny buds, controversial origin story but undeniably influential in modern Chinese black tea pricing.

Name: Laoshan Black
Story (Legend or background): Rare northern Chinese black tea from Shandong's Laoshan, snowy climate gives a surprisingly sweet mellow cup.

Name: Yingde Hong Cha
Story (Legend or background): Guangdong black tea district revived in the 1950s, bright red liquor suited to milk tea culture in Hong Kong.

Name: Jasmine Dragon Pearls
Story (Legend or background): Hand-rolled green pearls scented with jasmine flowers layer by layer, a Song-era tradition refined in Fuzhou.

Name: Jasmine Mo Li Hua Cha
Story (Legend or background): Base tea scented with jasmine sambac, Fujian developed industrial scenting that supplies teahouses worldwide.

Name: Rose Black Tea
Story (Legend or background): Modern scented blend popular in Chinese cafés, combines Qimen or Dian Hong base with red rose petals for romance gifting.

Name: Pu-erh Sheng – Yiwu Gushu
Story (Legend or background): Raw pu-erh from ancient trees in Yiwu, one of the Six Great Tea Mountains of Xishuangbanna trade routes since Qing times.

Name: Pu-erh Shou – Menghai Ripe
Story (Legend or background): Wo Dui fermentation invented in 1973 accelerates aging, Menghai Factory Recipe 7542 became the benchmark cooked pu-erh.

Name: Liu Bao Hei Cha
Story (Legend or background): Guangxi aged dark tea with betel-nut aroma, overseas Chinese in Southeast Asia drank it for humidity relief since the 19th century.

Name: Anhua Hei Cha
Story (Legend or background): Hunan dark tea pressed for horse-caravan trade on the Tea Horse Road, golden flowers (Eurotium) sometimes grow on bricks.

Name: Fuzhuan Brick Tea
Story (Legend or background): Brick tea with golden fungus prized on the frontier, Tibetan and Mongolian nomads boiled it with milk and salt for centuries.

Name: Tuocha
Story (Legend or background): Bowl-shaped pu-erh tuo easy to carry on the Tea Horse Road, default travel tea of Yunnan merchants and backpackers today.

Name: Pu-erh Bing Cha
Story (Legend or background): Disk cakes wrapped in paper for aging and speculation, 20th-century tea collectors treat vintages like wine futures.

Name: Chenpi Pu-erh
Story (Legend or background): Guangdong blend of ripe pu-erh stuffed in dried tangerine peel, aids digestion according to Cantonese dim sum culture.

Name: Gu Shu Hong
Story (Legend or background): Black tea processed from Yunnan gushu leaves, bridges red tea fashion with ancient-tree terroir storytelling.

Name: Huangjin Gui
Story (Legend or background): Wuyi rock tea cultivar with osmanthus-like perfume, name celebrates both color of liquor and cassia fragrance metaphor.
